hook.text: The UK auto-enrolled workers into pensions. Participation jumped from 55% to 90%. Nobody was forced.

buildup.text: Before auto-enrollment, workers had to actively sign up. Procrastination, complexity, and inertia kept millions.

discovery.text: Madrian and Shea showed auto-enrollment at one firm increased participation from 49% to 86%.

twist.text: The default contribution rate becomes an anchor. If auto-enrolled at 3%, most stay at 3% though 10% would serve them.

climax.text: Auto-enrollment is the most successful behavioral policy ever. But setting the right default rate matters as much.

punchline.text: Change the default and millions start saving. That simple.

quiz.question: What is the risk of auto-enrolling at a low contribution rate?
options: The low rate becomes an anchor and workers save less than they should
It violates workers' rights to choose

details.summary: Auto-enrollment switches pension participation from opt-in to opt-out, harnessing inertia and the default effect to dramatically increase retirement savings rates. In the UK, participation jumped from 61 to 92 percent after auto-enrollment was introduced.
details.whyItMatters: Auto-enrollment is the signature success story of behavioral public policy. It demonstrates that changing the default rather than the incentive can transform outcomes at massive scale with minimal cost and no restriction of freedom.
takeaways: Switching to opt-out increased UK pension participation from 61 to 92 percent
Inertia and default bias do the heavy lifting without forcing anyone
Auto-enrollment preserves freedom of choice while dramatically improving outcomes

faq.question: Why does auto-enrollment work so well for pensions?
faq.answer: Most people intend to save for retirement but procrastinate. Auto-enrollment eliminates the need for action. Since opting out requires effort, inertia keeps people enrolled. The default aligns with what people say they want but fail to do.

faq.question: Do people who are auto-enrolled save enough?
faq.answer: Often not. Default contribution rates are typically set low to minimize opt-outs. Programs like Save More Tomorrow address this by auto-escalating contributions with future raises, increasing savings gradually without reducing take-home pay.
